chapter_summary:
Effective network interface configuration is a cornerstone of any robust Linux system, especially in enterprise settings where high availability and specific network topologies are critical. While basic IP address assignment might seem straightforward, an LPIC-2 level engineer needs to master dynamic and persistent configurations, as well as advanced concepts like bonding and bridging.

The `ip` command is the modern, versatile utility for managing network interfaces, replacing older commands like `ifconfig` and `route`. To assign an IP address to an interface, for example, `ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0` will temporarily configure `eth0`. To bring an interface up or down, you'd use `ip link set eth0 up` or `ip link set eth0 down`. It's crucial to remember that changes made with the `ip` command are typically not persistent across reboots. For persistent configuration, you must modify system configuration files or use a network management service.

Modern Linux distributions often rely on NetworkManager for managing network connections. NetworkManager provides a consistent interface for configuring network settings, whether the system is a desktop or a server. The `nmcli` (NetworkManager Command Line Interface) tool is indispensable for server administrators. With `nmcli`, you can list connections (`nmcli connection show`), add new connections (`nmcli connection add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name my-eth0 ip4 192.168.1.10/24 gw4 192.168.1.1`), modify existing ones (`nmcli connection modify my-eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8"`), and activate/deactivate them (`nmcli connection up my-eth0`). For those who prefer a text-based user interface, `nmtui` offers an interactive menu-driven approach to configure NetworkManager connections. Understanding how to use `nmcli` is vital for scripting and automating network configurations on headless servers.

For persistent configurations without NetworkManager, or in specific scenarios, you might interact directly with configuration files. On Red Hat-based systems (RHEL, CentOS, Fedora), network configurations are traditionally stored in `/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-*` files. Each interface or connection typically has its own file, e.g., `ifcfg-eth0`. A typical `ifcfg-eth0` file might contain `BOOTPROTO=static`, `IPADDR=192.168.1.10`, `NETMASK=255.255.255.0`, `GATEWAY=192.168.1.1`, `DNS1=8.8.8.8`, and `ONBOOT=yes`. After modifying these files, you usually need to restart the network service or the specific interface using `systemctl restart network` or `nmcli connection reload && nmcli connection up my-eth0`. Debian-based systems (Ubuntu, Debian) historically use `/etc/network/interfaces`. A stanza for a static IP would look like:
```
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet static
    address 192.168.1.10
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    gateway 192.168.1.1
    dns-nameservers 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
```
After editing, `systemctl restart networking` or `ifup eth0` would apply the changes. Newer distributions might also use `netplan` for configuration, which generates backend configuration for NetworkManager or systemd-networkd from YAML files in `/etc/netplan/*.yaml`.

Beyond basic IP settings, an LPIC-2 engineer must be proficient in network bonding (also known as teaming or link aggregation) and bridging. Network bonding combines multiple physical network interfaces into a single logical interface, providing redundancy (failover) and/or increased throughput. This is critical for high-availability services where network downtime is unacceptable. For example, if one physical NIC fails, traffic seamlessly switches to the other. To configure bonding with `nmcli`, you would create a bond master connection and then add slave connections:
```bash
nmcli connection add type bond con-name mybond ifname bond0 mode active-backup ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.20/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth0-slave ifname eth0 master mybond
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth1-slave ifname eth1 master mybond
nmcli connection up mybond
```
This creates `bond0` in `active-backup` mode, meaning one interface is active and the other is a standby. Other modes include `balance-rr` (round-robin) for load balancing.

Network bridging, on the other hand, connects multiple network segments at the data link layer, effectively creating a software switch. This is commonly used in virtualization environments, where virtual machines need to share a physical network interface to communicate with the external network. A bridge interface (`br0`) acts as a virtual switch, and physical interfaces (like `eth0`) and virtual interfaces (from VMs) can be attached to it. With `nmcli`, you might configure a bridge like this:
```bash
nmcli connection add type bridge con-name mybridge ifname br0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.30/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth0-bridge-slave ifname eth0 master mybridge
nmcli connection up mybridge
```
This sets up `br0` and adds `eth0` as a port to it. VMs can then be configured to use `br0` for their networking.

Common mistakes include forgetting to make changes persistent, which leads to configurations being lost after a reboot. Always verify your changes with `ip addr show` and `ip route show` after applying them. When working with bonding or bridging, ensure that the underlying physical interfaces are not already configured with an IP address, as they will be managed by the bond or bridge master. Incorrect bonding modes can lead to performance issues or unexpected failover behavior. When troubleshooting, always check the system logs (`journalctl -u NetworkManager` or `dmesg`) for errors related to network interface initialization. Safety note: When modifying network configurations on a remote server, always have a backup plan (e.g., a console connection or out-of-band management) to avoid locking yourself out of the system. Test changes incrementally and verify connectivity after each step.

Module 3›Chapter 3.1›The `ip` Command

The `ip` Command: Modern Network Control

Replacing Legacy Tools for Interface Management

Key Definition

The ip command is a powerful, unified command-line utility in Linux for managing network interfaces, IP addresses, routing tables, and network tunnels. It's part of the `iproute2` suite and is the standard for modern network configuration.

Key Takeaway

Embrace the `ip` command for all network configuration tasks; it offers a consistent and powerful interface over older, fragmented tools.

Why it Matters
  • Unified Interface: Manages all network aspects from a single command.
  • Efficiency: Designed for better performance and scalability in large networks.
  • Modern Standard: The default tool in contemporary Linux distributions.
  • Scripting Friendly: Its consistent output is ideal for automation scripts.
`ip` vs. `ifconfig`
`ip` Command`ifconfig` (Legacy)
Modern, comprehensiveOlder, limited scope
Manages interfaces, routes, tunnelsPrimarily interfaces, basic routes
Part of `iproute2`Part of `net-tools`
Recommended for new systemsDeprecated in many distros

narration.text: Let's dive into practical application of the ip command for temporary network configuration. To assign an IP address to an interface, you use ip addr add followed by the IP address in CIDR notation and the device name. For example, ip addr add 192.168.1.10 slash 24 dev eth0 will configure eth0 with that specific IP. This change is immediate, allowing you to test connectivity or make quick adjustments. Similarly, managing the state of an interface, bringing it up or down, is done with ip link set. Using ip link set eth0 up activates the interface, while ip link set eth0 down deactivates it. It's crucial to remember that these changes are temporary; they will not persist across a system reboot. This is a common misconception, as many expect these runtime changes to be permanent. Always verify your configuration with ip addr show after making changes to ensure they've been applied correctly. This temporary nature makes ip ideal for troubleshooting or one-off tasks, but not for permanent system configurations. Module 3›Chapter 3.1›Temporary IP Config

Temporary IP Configuration with `ip`

Assigning Addresses and Managing Interface States

Command Syntax
# Assign IP address
ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0

# Bring interface up
ip link set eth0 up

# Bring interface down
ip link set eth0 down

# Verify configuration
ip addr show eth0
Key Takeaway

`ip` command changes are immediate but temporary; they do not persist across reboots without additional configuration.

Important Considerations
  • Non-Persistent: Changes are lost after a reboot.
  • Immediate Effect: Useful for testing and troubleshooting.
  • Device Naming: `eth0`, `enp0s3`, etc., refer to specific network interfaces.
  • CIDR Notation: `/24` specifies the subnet mask (e.g., 255.255.255.0).
Common Mistake

Forgetting that `ip` command changes are temporary. Always remember to implement persistent configuration methods for production systems to avoid network downtime after a reboot.

Module 3›Chapter 3.1›NetworkManager

Introducing NetworkManager

The Dynamic Network Configuration Daemon

What is NetworkManager?

NetworkManager is a system daemon that manages network connections, providing a consistent interface for configuring network settings across various types of connections (wired, wireless, VPNs). It aims to keep network devices and connections up and active whenever possible.

Key Takeaway

NetworkManager simplifies complex network configurations and ensures persistent, reliable connectivity across Linux systems.

Key Benefits
  • Consistency: Unified approach for all connection types.
  • Persistence: Configurations survive reboots automatically.
  • Automation: Command-line tools (`nmcli`) for scripting.
  • Dynamic Management: Handles network changes on the fly.
  • User-Friendly: Graphical and text-based interfaces (`nmtui`).
Tools for Interaction

`nmcli`

NetworkManager Command Line Interface for scripting and server management.

`nmtui`

NetworkManager Text User Interface for interactive, menu-driven configuration.

narration.text: The nmcli tool, or NetworkManager Command Line Interface, is an indispensable utility for server administrators. It allows you to interact with NetworkManager directly from the terminal, making it perfect for scripting and automating network configurations. With nmcli, you can perform a wide range of tasks, from simply listing active connections to adding complex new ones. For example, nmcli connection show provides an overview of all configured network connections. To add a new static Ethernet connection, you'd use nmcli connection add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name my-eth0 ip4 192.168.1.10 slash 24 gw4 192.168.1.1. This command creates a new connection profile named 'my-eth0' for the eth0 interface with a static IP and gateway. You can then modify existing connections, perhaps to add a DNS server, using nmcli connection modify my-eth0 ipv4. dns '8.8.8.8'. Finally, to apply these changes, you activate the connection with nmcli connection up my-eth0. Understanding nmcli is vital for maintaining consistent network settings on headless servers and for integrating network management into larger automation workflows. Module 3›Chapter 3.1›`nmcli` Management

Managing Connections with `nmcli`

Scripting and Automating Network Configurations

Key `nmcli` Commands
# List all connections
nmcli connection show

# Add a new static Ethernet connection
nmcli connection add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name my-eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1

# Modify an existing connection (e.g., add DNS)
nmcli connection modify my-eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8"

# Activate a connection
nmcli connection up my-eth0

# Deactivate a connection
nmcli connection down my-eth0
Key Takeaway

`nmcli` is essential for programmatic network management, offering granular control over connections for automation and server administration.

`nmcli` Workflow
  • Show: View existing connections and their states.
  • Add: Create new connection profiles for various network types.
  • Modify: Adjust parameters of existing connections.
  • Up/Down: Activate or deactivate connections to apply changes.
  • Delete: Remove unwanted connection profiles.
`nmtui` for Interactive Use

For those who prefer a text-based graphical interface, `nmtui` provides an interactive, menu-driven way to configure NetworkManager connections. It's user-friendly for quick, manual adjustments without needing to remember complex `nmcli` syntax.

Module 3›Chapter 3.1›Red Hat Persistence

Persistent Configuration: Red Hat Systems

Managing Network Settings with `ifcfg-*` Files

Example `ifcfg-eth0` File
TYPE=Ethernet
BOOTPROTO=static
NAME=eth0
DEVICE=eth0
ONBOOT=yes
IPADDR=192.168.1.10
NETMASK=255.255.255.0
GATEWAY=192.168.1.1
DNS1=8.8.8.8
Key Takeaway

`ifcfg-*` files provide granular, persistent control over network interfaces on Red Hat systems, but require service restarts to apply changes.

Key Parameters
  • `BOOTPROTO`: `static`, `dhcp`, `none`.
  • `ONBOOT`: `yes` to activate at boot, `no` otherwise.
  • `IPADDR`, `NETMASK`, `GATEWAY`: Define static IP settings.
  • `DNS1`, `DNS2`: Specify DNS servers.
  • `NAME`, `DEVICE`: Logical and physical interface names.
Applying Changes

After editing `ifcfg-*` files, you must restart the network service (`systemctl restart network`) or reload the specific NetworkManager connection (`nmcli connection reload && nmcli connection up my-eth0`) for changes to take effect.

Within this stanza, you define the address, netmask, gateway, and dns-nameservers. After making changes to this file, you would typically apply them using systemctl restart networking or ifup eth0. However, newer distributions are increasingly adopting netplan for network configuration. Netplan uses YAML files, typically found in slash etc slash netplan slash asterisk. yaml, to define network settings in a more declarative way. It then generates backend configurations for either NetworkManager or systemd-networkd. This approach offers a more unified and flexible way to manage network settings across different Linux systems. Understanding both traditional and modern approaches ensures you can manage network persistence regardless of the distribution. Module 3›Chapter 3.1›Debian & Netplan

Persistent Configuration: Debian & Netplan

Alternative Approaches to Network Persistence

Debian `/etc/network/interfaces`
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet static
    address 192.168.1.10
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    gateway 192.168.1.1
    dns-nameservers 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
Key Takeaway

Different distributions use distinct configuration files for persistence; `netplan` offers a modern, unified approach via YAML.

Netplan Configuration (`.yaml`)
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: NetworkManager
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      dhcp4: no
      addresses: [192.168.1.10/24]
      gateway4: 192.168.1.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4]
Applying Netplan Changes

After modifying a Netplan YAML file, apply the changes using sudo netplan apply. Netplan then generates the necessary backend configuration for NetworkManager or systemd-networkd.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.1›Network Bonding

Network Bonding: High Availability & Throughput

Combining Interfaces for Redundancy and Performance

What is Network Bonding?

Network bonding (also known as teaming or link aggregation) is a technique that combines multiple physical network interfaces into a single logical interface. This provides redundancy (failover) and/or increased throughput, crucial for high-availability services.

Key Takeaway

Bonding enhances network reliability and performance by creating resilient, aggregated links from multiple physical interfaces.

Benefits of Bonding
  • High Availability: Automatic failover if a physical link fails.
  • Increased Throughput: Distributes traffic across multiple links (depending on mode).
  • Load Balancing: Optimizes network utilization.
  • Redundancy: Prevents single points of failure in network connectivity.
Common Bonding Modes

`active-backup`

One interface is active, others are standby. Provides failover.

`balance-rr`

Round-robin policy for load balancing and fault tolerance.

narration.text: Configuring network bonding using nmcli involves creating a bond master connection and then adding physical interfaces as slave connections to it. Let's walk through setting up an active-backup bond, which is ideal for fault tolerance. First, you create the bond master connection, specifying its type as bond, giving it a connection name like mybond, and an interface name such as bond0. Crucially, you define the mode as active-backup and assign an IP address. For example, nmcli connection add type bond con-name mybond ifname bond0 mode active-backup ipv4. method manual ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.20 slash 24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1. Once the master is created, you add your physical interfaces, like eth0 and eth1, as slave connections. These are ethernet type connections, and you link them to the master using master mybond. For instance, nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth0-slave ifname eth0 master mybond. After adding all slaves, you activate the bond master connection with nmcli connection up mybond. It's important to ensure the physical interfaces are not already configured with an IP address, as the bond master will manage their IP. This setup provides seamless failover, ensuring continuous network connectivity.

Module 3›Chapter 3.1›`nmcli` Bonding

Configuring Bonding with `nmcli`

Step-by-Step `active-backup` Mode Implementation

`nmcli` Bonding Commands
# 1. Create bond master connection (active-backup mode)
nmcli connection add type bond con-name mybond ifname bond0 mode active-backup ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.20/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1

# 2. Add eth0 as a slave to the bond
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth0-slave ifname eth0 master mybond

# 3. Add eth1 as a slave to the bond
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth1-slave ifname eth1 master mybond

# 4. Activate the bond connection
nmcli connection up mybond

# 5. Verify bond status
nmcli connection show mybond
ip addr show bond0
Key Takeaway

`nmcli` simplifies bonding setup by defining a master connection and attaching physical interfaces as slaves, enabling robust failover.

Bonding Process Flow
Step 1

Define Bond Master (e.g., `bond0`) with desired mode.

Step 2

Add Physical NICs (e.g., `eth0`, `eth1`) as slaves.

Step 3

Activate the Bond Master connection.

Step 4

Verify connectivity and failover functionality.

Important Note

Ensure physical interfaces intended for bonding are not already configured with IP addresses; the bond master will manage their IP settings.

narration.text: Network bridging is another advanced configuration crucial for virtualization environments. It connects multiple network segments at the data link layer, essentially creating a software switch. This virtual switch, often named br0, allows virtual machines to share a single physical network interface to communicate with the external network. Imagine a physical server hosting several virtual machines; without bridging, each VM would need its own dedicated physical NIC, which is often impractical. With a bridge, the physical interface, say eth0, becomes a port on the virtual switch br0. The VMs then connect to br0, allowing them to communicate with each other and with the external network as if they were directly connected to a physical switch. This setup simplifies network management for virtualized hosts, enabling efficient resource sharing and flexible network topologies for your virtualized infrastructure. It's a fundamental concept for anyone managing virtualized Linux systems. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.1›Network Bridging

Network Bridging: Virtualization Essentials

Creating a Software Switch for Virtual Machines

What is Network Bridging?

Network bridging connects multiple network segments at the data link layer, effectively creating a software-based virtual switch. This is commonly used in virtualization environments to allow virtual machines to share a physical network interface and communicate with the external network.

Key Takeaway

Bridging is fundamental for virtualization, enabling VMs to share physical network resources and communicate seamlessly.

Bridging in Virtualization
  • Shared Access: VMs share a single physical NIC.
  • Virtual Switch: The bridge (`br0`) acts as a layer 2 switch.
  • External Communication: VMs can reach the external network.
  • Inter-VM Communication: VMs on the same bridge can communicate directly.
  • Simplified Management: Reduces the need for multiple physical interfaces.
Bridge Components

Bridge Interface (`br0`)

The virtual switch itself, configured with an IP address.

Physical Interface (e.g., `eth0`)

Added as a port to the bridge, connecting it to the physical network.

Virtual Machine Interfaces

Connect to the bridge, gaining network access.

screens.title: Configuring Bridging with `nmcli`
screens.subtitle: Setting Up a Virtual Switch for VMs

narration.text: Just like with bonding, nmcli simplifies the configuration of network bridges. To set up a bridge, you first create the bridge master connection. This involves specifying type bridge, giving it a connection name like mybridge, and an interface name such as br0. You then assign an IP address to this bridge interface, for example, nmcli connection add type bridge con-name mybridge ifname br0 ipv4. method manual ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.30 slash 24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1. This command establishes the virtual switch itself. Next, you add your physical network interface, such as eth0, as a slave port to this bridge. This is done by creating an ethernet type connection and linking it to the bridge master using master mybridge. For instance, nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth0-bridge-slave ifname eth0 master mybridge. Once the physical interface is added as a port, you activate the bridge connection with nmcli connection up mybridge. After activation, virtual machines can be configured to use br0 for their networking, allowing them to communicate through the physical eth0 interface. Remember to verify your configuration using ip addr show br0 and nmcli connection show to ensure everything is set up correctly. This process is fundamental for creating flexible and scalable virtualized environments.

Setting Up a Virtual Switch for VMs

`nmcli` Bridging Commands

nmcli connection add type bridge con-name mybridge ifname br0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.30/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1

# 2. Add eth0 as a slave port to the bridge
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name eth0-bridge-slave ifname eth0 master mybridge

# 3. Activate the bridge connection
nmcli connection up mybridge

# 4. Verify bridge status
nmcli connection show mybridge
ip addr show br0
Key Takeaway

`nmcli` facilitates bridge creation by defining a master and adding physical interfaces as ports, enabling shared network access for VMs.

Bridging Process Flow
Step 1

Define Bridge Master (e.g., `br0`) with IP settings.

Step 2

Step 3

Step 4

Troubleshooting Tip

Always check system logs (`journalctl -u NetworkManager` or `dmesg`) for errors if a bridge fails to activate or function as expected.

Key Concepts: Core Tools

Essential Utilities for Network Management

`ip` Command

The primary modern utility for configuring and managing network interfaces, IP addresses, and routing tables.

NetworkManager

A dynamic network configuration daemon and set of tools that manages network connections on Linux systems.

`nmcli`

NetworkManager Command Line Interface, used for scripting and managing network connections from the terminal.

Chapter Summary

Mastering these tools allows for both immediate diagnostics and robust, persistent network configurations across diverse Linux environments.

narration.text: Continuing our review of key concepts, let's focus on advanced techniques and persistence. Network bonding, also known as teaming or link aggregation, is a powerful method for combining multiple physical network interfaces into a single logical one. This is vital for achieving high availability through failover and increasing throughput, making your network infrastructure more resilient. Then we have network bridging, which creates a software switch to connect multiple network segments. This is particularly important in virtualization, allowing virtual machines to efficiently share a physical network interface and communicate externally. Finally, understanding persistent configuration is paramount. These are the settings that survive a system reboot, typically stored in specific configuration files like slash etc slash sysconfig slash network-scripts slash ifcfg- asterisk on Red Hat systems, slash etc slash network slash interfaces on Debian, or modern YAML files in slash etc slash netplan. Ensuring your configurations are persistent is key to maintaining stable and reliable systems over time.

Key Concepts: Advanced & Persistence

Critical Techniques for Enterprise Networking

Bonding (Teaming)

Combining multiple physical network interfaces into a single logical interface for redundancy, load balancing, or increased throughput.

Bridging

Creating a software switch that connects multiple network segments, commonly used for virtualization to allow VMs to share a physical NIC.

Persistent Configuration

Settings that survive a system reboot, typically stored in configuration files like `/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-*`, `/etc/network/interfaces`, or `/etc/netplan/*.yaml`.

Chapter Summary

These advanced techniques and an understanding of persistent configuration methods are vital for building and maintaining robust, high-performance Linux network infrastructures.
